Investor guide

How to calculate cash flow on a rental property

From gross rent to what's left after vacancy, expenses and the mortgage, using a $600,000 condo as the example.

Ali Bayat
Figures checked against the sources below on November 21, 2026
Published November 21, 2026
3-minute readFor investorsWorked example
The short version
  • Cash flow = rent − vacancy − operating expenses − mortgage payments.
  • At 20% down and today's rates, many GTA condos are cash-flow negative.
  • Part of every payment pays down the loan. That's equity, but it isn't cash in your pocket.

01Where $31,800 of rent goes

Example: a $600,000 condo (the GTA average condo apartment sold for $621,400 in October 2026, per TRREB), 20% down, $2,650/month rent. Rent, fees and the rate are assumptions for illustration.

02The same deal, three ways

−$1,061Per month, cash flowWhat you top up from your own pocket
$10,697Loan paid down, year 1Part of your payments builds equity
−$2,037Cash flow + paydownThe real cost of holding, before any price change

03Expenses people forget

  • VacancyEven one month empty is 8% of a year's rent.
  • Repairs and replacementsAppliances, flooring, paint between tenants.
  • Special assessmentsCondo buildings can levy owners for major repairs.
  • Closing costsLand transfer tax and legal fees come out of your cash up front.
Ali's take

Negative cash flow isn't automatically a bad deal, but you should know the exact monthly number before you buy, and be sure you can carry it if rates rise.
